# Elastic Load Balancing: say it

<!-- speak:start id=elb-s01 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** Application Load Balancer or Network Load Balancer: what decides it for a web application like ours?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Both spread traffic. The Application Load Balancer reads each web request and routes by path. The Network Load Balancer gives fixed IP addresses.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both spread traffic over your instances. The difference is what they read.

It works like this. The Application Load Balancer reads each HTTP request.

Its rules can send each URL path to a different group of instances.

AWS recommends it for HTTP traffic and flexible application management.

The Network Load Balancer works lower down, on TCP and UDP connections.

It never sees the URL, but it gives you static IP addresses and extreme performance.

The thing to watch is fixed IP addresses.

An Application Load Balancer has no static or Elastic IP addresses.

If you need both, a Network Load Balancer can forward to an Application Load Balancer.

In your case, it's a web application, and you'll route by path later.

So I'd choose the Application Load Balancer.

Does any customer need to allow-list fixed IP addresses for your site?

**Skeleton.** both spread, read differently / Application reads HTTP, routes path / Network: TCP, static IPs / fixed IPs: Network in front

**Must say.**

- An Application Load Balancer can forward requests based on the URL path, so each service gets its own route.
- AWS recommends an Application Load Balancer for HTTP requests and for flexible application management.
- AWS recommends a Network Load Balancer for TCP and UDP load balancing, extreme performance and a static IP address.
- Of the load balancer types, only the Network Load Balancer has static or Elastic IP addresses.

**Do not say.**

- "a Network Load Balancer can route by URL path". Say: The Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 and does not read the URL. Path rules need the layer 7 Application Load Balancer.
- "you can attach an Elastic IP address to the Application Load Balancer". Say: Only the Network Load Balancer has static or Elastic IP addresses.
- "the Network Load Balancer is always the better choice because it's faster". Say: AWS recommends the Application Load Balancer when you load balance HTTP requests or need flexible application management.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can we have fixed IP addresses and path routing together? Yes. Forward traffic from a Network Load Balancer to the Application Load Balancer. The Network Load Balancer gives the static IP addresses, and the Application Load Balancer keeps its request-based routing.
- Which one helps us block attacks on the web application? The Application Load Balancer integrates with AWS WAF. WAF rules on IP addresses, HTTP headers and URI strings can block, allow, or monitor (count) web requests.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=elb-s03 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** Our auditor says patient data must be encrypted all the way to the servers. Is HTTPS on the load balancer enough?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Not by itself. The load balancer decrypts the request. Add HTTPS to the instances too, or let a Network Load Balancer pass TLS through.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: not by itself.

It works like this. The HTTPS listener ends the TLS connection at the load balancer.

The load balancer decrypts the request there, before it sends it on.

So you add a second encrypted hop: an HTTPS target group to your instances.

If your instances must do the decryption, use a Network Load Balancer instead.

Its TCP listener passes the encrypted traffic through to the instances.

The thing to watch is the certificate on the instances.

The Application Load Balancer encrypts that second hop, but it doesn't validate the certificate.

So you get encryption, but no check of which instance it's talking to.

In your case, I'd use HTTPS on both hops of the Application Load Balancer.

Will your auditor accept that the load balancer sees the request decrypted for a moment?

**Skeleton.** listener decrypts at load balancer / second hop: HTTPS target group / pass-through: Network Load Balancer / target certificate not validated

**Must say.**

- The load balancer uses its certificate to terminate the front-end connection and decrypt requests before it sends them to the targets.
- With an HTTPS target group, the load balancer opens TLS connections to the targets with certificates that you install on the targets.
- If the targets must decrypt the traffic, a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443 passes it through without decrypting it.
- The Application Load Balancer does not validate the target certificates; only encryption is supported to the back ends, not server authentication.

**Do not say.**

- "HTTPS on the load balancer encrypts everything all the way to the instances". Say: The load balancer decrypts requests from clients before it sends them to the targets. The second hop needs its own HTTPS.
- "the load balancer checks the certificate on the instance". Say: The load balancer does not validate the target certificates, so self-signed or expired certificates work.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can we use self-signed certificates on the instances? Yes. The load balancer does not validate these certificates, so you can use self-signed certificates or certificates that have expired.
- Doesn't decryption on the instances cost us compute? That's the trade-off. When the load balancer terminates TLS, it performs the work of encrypting and decrypting instead of each EC2 instance. With a pass-through, each instance does that work.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=elb-s02 -->
### Prompt 3

**A customer asks.** Our customer's firewall team wants fixed IP addresses for our API. We use an Application Load Balancer. What do we do?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Keep the Application Load Balancer. Put a Network Load Balancer in front of it. Or use AWS Global Accelerator.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: keep your Application Load Balancer and add fixed addresses.

It works like this. An Application Load Balancer has no static or Elastic IP addresses.

As traffic changes, AWS scales it and updates its DNS record.

So don't give out its IP addresses. They can change.

The first option is a Network Load Balancer in front.

It has a static IP address in each Availability Zone.

It forwards traffic to your Application Load Balancer, so your path rules stay.

The other option is AWS Global Accelerator, with its own static IP addresses.

The thing to watch is your future Regions.

Global Accelerator can spread traffic over load balancers in more than one Region.

In your case, with one Region, the Network Load Balancer is enough.

Will your API run in one Region only, or in several?

**Skeleton.** keep it, add fixed addresses / its own addresses change / Network Load Balancer in front / Global Accelerator for many Regions

**Must say.**

- Of the load balancer types, only the Network Load Balancer has static or Elastic IP addresses.
- Elastic Load Balancing scales the load balancer and updates its DNS entry, so the IP addresses can be remapped quickly.
- A Network Load Balancer with a static IP address per Availability Zone can forward traffic to the Application Load Balancer, which keeps its layer 7 routing.
- AWS Global Accelerator gives static IP addresses that serve as fixed endpoints for the load balancer.

**Do not say.**

- "attach an Elastic IP address to the Application Load Balancer". Say: Only the Network Load Balancer has static or Elastic IP addresses.
- "give them the current IP addresses, they don't change". Say: Elastic Load Balancing scales the load balancer and updates its DNS entry, so the IP addresses can be remapped quickly.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Why should clients use the DNS name and not the addresses? The load balancer scales as traffic changes, and its DNS entry has a time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds, so the IP addresses can be remapped quickly.
- Does Global Accelerator help against attacks too? AWS Global Accelerator is protected by Shield Standard, which helps reduce downtime and latency from DDoS attacks.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=elb-s04 -->
### Prompt 4

**A customer asks.** If one AWS data center fails during the launch, will our customers notice?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Mostly not. The load balancer runs in each Availability Zone. It sends users only to healthy instances, so the other zones take over.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: most customers won't notice.

It works like this. Your app runs in several Availability Zones.

An Availability Zone is one or more separate data centers with redundant power and networking.

The load balancer has a node in each of those zones.

It checks the health of every instance and sends users only to healthy ones.

If one zone fails, the instances there fail their health checks.

Then the load balancer sends new requests to the instances in the other zones.

The thing to watch is the time the health checks need to notice a failure.

Some requests to the failed instances can fail in that time.

And the other zones must carry the extra traffic.

In your case, each zone runs web instances behind the load balancer.

Can the other zones carry the launch traffic on their own?

**Skeleton.** node in each zone / health checks pick healthy instances / other zones take the requests / some requests fail before detection

**Must say.**

- Elastic Load Balancing creates a load balancer node in each Availability Zone that you enable.
- The load balancer monitors the health of its registered targets and routes traffic only to the healthy targets.
- Before the load balancer discovers that an instance is unhealthy, some requests to that instance fail.
- Cross-zone load balancing is on by default for an Application Load Balancer, so each node uses the registered targets in all enabled Availability Zones.

**Do not say.**

- "nobody will notice anything". Say: Before the load balancer discovers that an instance is unhealthy, some requests to that instance fail.
- "the load balancer moves us to another Region". Say: The load balancer has a node in each Availability Zone that you enable, and it routes to the healthy targets there.
- "the load balancer replaces the broken instances". Say: The load balancer stops sending traffic to them. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling replaces an unhealthy instance.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can we move traffic away from a zone ourselves if it behaves strangely? Yes. Zonal shift, a feature of Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC), moves the traffic away from an impaired Availability Zone with a single action.
- Does the load balancer also replace the broken instances? No. It stops sending traffic to them. With ELB health checks turned on in an Auto Scaling group, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling replaces the unhealthy instance.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->
